# **Stargazer Mission Mode: Translating Real Lunar Programme Challenges into Playable Systems** **Generated by MiroThinker2026-11-14**

---

**1Part 1 — Executive Summary**

Establishing a sustainable human presence on the Moon is not a single “base-building” event but a decades‑long architecture: dozens of robotic precursors, incremental power and communications infrastructure, progressive habitat capabilities, and a constant struggle with schedule, budget, and technology risk. NASA’s Moon to Mars Architecture and Moon Base plans explicitly adopt a phased, iterative approach at the lunar south pole, beginning with many robotic landings through \~2029, then building semi‑habitable infrastructure and finally aiming for long‑duration, resource‑supported operations in the 2030s and beyond.[**\[1\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/reference/moonbase-phases/)**[\[2\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/lunar/strategies/resources/M2M_ACR2025_WhyMoonAndMars_v2.pdf)[\[3\]](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/moon-base-architecture-users-guide.pdf)**

The south pole itself is an intrinsically game‑friendly environment: terrain is rugged and heavily cratered, crater floors sit in permanent shadow while nearby ridges can be illuminated for \>70–90% of a lunar year, and Earth is only directly visible from polar sites for roughly half of each 29.5‑day synodic month, with visibility patterns not synchronized with illumination.[**\[4\]**](https://www.planetary.org/space-images/shackleton-crater-illumination)**[\[5\]](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2018JE005668)[\[6\]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/319406298_Visibility_and_Lighting_Conditions_on_a_Modelled_Lunar_Surface)[\[7\]](https://www.nasa.gov/reference/moonbase-environment/)** This forces real missions to trade off power vs communications vs safety in landing‑site selection, and to consider relay satellites and energy storage from the outset.[**\[5\]**](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2018JE005668)**[\[6\]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/319406298_Visibility_and_Lighting_Conditions_on_a_Modelled_Lunar_Surface)[\[8\]](https://www.nasa.gov/space-communications-and-navigation/lunar-communications-relay-and-navigation-services/)**

Real programmes are dominated by constraints and dependencies rather than by individual heroic missions. Artemis and CLPS missions have experienced substantial delays and cost growth; an official NASA Inspector General report records average CLPS task‑order cost overruns of \~26% and average schedule slippage of \~14 months, and Artemis human‑landing system providers are already behind schedule.[**\[9\]**](https://oig.nasa.gov/docs/IG-24-011.pdf)**[\[10\]](https://oig.nasa.gov/docs/IG-23-003.pdf)[\[11\]](https://oig.nasa.gov/news/artemis-lander-program-faces-schedule-delays-and-unmitigated-crew-safety-risks/)** NASA explicitly uses Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs) to decide when new systems can be trusted for critical roles, and its lunar architecture documents list key “unfilled” functional gaps for power and habitats—pressurised surface habitats for both short and longer durations are still requirements rather than existing capabilities.[**\[3\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/moon-base-architecture-users-guide.pdf)**[\[12\]](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/trl.pdf)**

The strongest opportunity for Stargazer is therefore **not** to simulate every subsystem in detail, but to put players in the role of an architecture manager navigating real‑world constraints:

* Choosing landing regions and arrival dates under real sun/Earth visibility and terrain constraints (leveraging the existing engine).  
* Sequencing robotic and crewed missions to raise TRLs and close specific capability gaps (e.g., power, comms, habitats, ISRU).  
* Managing schedules, budgets, and risk exposure as delays cascade across interdependent projects.  
* Experiencing how south‑pole lighting and Earth visibility shape decisions about power systems, relay infrastructure, and base layout.

A **hybrid programme‑manager \+ mission‑level simulator** (Option 3\) best exploits Stargazer’s strengths: strategic planning on a multi‑year calendar, punctuated by short, high‑leverage “mission operations” scenes that use the 3D south‑pole environment, terrain horizon, and visibility timelines to make the consequences of architectural choices tangible.

---

**2Part 2 — The Road to a Lunar Colony**

### **2.1 Phased Architectures in Real Plans**

**Real lunar strategies use phased, capability‑building roadmaps rather than a fixed end‑state “colony design”.** NASA’s Moon to Mars Architecture and Moon Base user guides describe three broad phases at the south pole: Phase I (now through \~2029) with \>20 robotic landings validating components; Phase II (\~2029–2032) building semi‑habitable infrastructure (pressurised rover, early habitats, logistics); and Phase III (2032+) pursuing sustained presence with permanent habitats, fission power, and ISRU for oxygen and water.[**\[1\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/reference/moonbase-phases/)**[\[2\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/lunar/strategies/resources/M2M_ACR2025_WhyMoonAndMars_v2.pdf)[\[3\]](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/moon-base-architecture-users-guide.pdf)[\[13\]](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/04/260425123456.htm)**

This architecture intentionally leaves the “final colony” under‑specified: documents emphasise closing functional gaps (power at south pole, distributed power, short‑ and long‑duration pressurised habitats, etc.) rather than a single monolithic base.[**\[3\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/moon-base-architecture-users-guide.pdf) For Stargazer, this argues for progression defined by **capabilities and functions** (what you can safely do on the surface) rather than by arbitrary building counts.

### **2.2 Reconnaissance and Site Selection**

**Initial phases focus on mapping, illumination and Earth‑visibility analysis, and hazard characterization.** Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter’s LOLA instrument provides global digital elevation models (DEMs) at \~30 m resolution and enhanced \~5 m products at the poles, supporting slope, roughness, and horizon calculations for candidate landing sites.[**\[14\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/lro/lola/)

South‑pole site selection studies and Artemis III analyses emphasise:

* Terrain slope and roughness for safe landings (goal \~≤5–8° slopes within a safety radius and avoidance of large boulders and fresh craters).[**\[15\]**](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/17/9/1579)**[\[16\]](https://aerospaceamerica.aiaa.org/features/the-choice/)**  
* Illumination fraction and continuity on ridges and crater rims (some peaks near Shackleton Crater reach \~94% annual illumination).[**\[4\]**](https://www.planetary.org/space-images/shackleton-crater-illumination)**[\[17\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0032063318302421)**  
* Distribution of permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) that may host water ice but are cold, dark, and hazardous.[**\[18\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/science-research/science-at-nasa/2006/06nov_moonwater/)**[\[19\]](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-020-01222-x)**  
* Earth visibility patterns (approximately half the synodic month, varying with local topography and not synchronized with lighting).[**\[5\]**](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2018JE005668)**[\[6\]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/319406298_Visibility_and_Lighting_Conditions_on_a_Modelled_Lunar_Surface)[\[7\]](https://www.nasa.gov/reference/moonbase-environment/)**

Dependencies: high‑resolution topography, solar and Earth ephemerides, hazard detection algorithms.

Delays: incomplete data (especially for small‑scale hazards), evolving vehicle performance, and late‑breaking science priorities can cause site re‑trades.

**Game objective hook:** In an early campaign phase, the player uses Stargazer’s 3D scene and horizon‑based visibility tools to:

* Evaluate candidate sites for illumination, Earth visibility, and slope.  
* Choose initial “survey zones” that trade scientific interest (near PSRs) against landing safety and power continuity.  
* Commit to a region, locking in future mission delta‑v and communications requirements.

### **2.3 Robotic Exploration and Scientific Surveys**

**Real programmes plan many robotic landings before sustained crew presence.** Moon Base Phase I calls for more than twenty robotic landings through 2029 to characterise environment, test technologies, and pre‑deploy infrastructure.[**\[1\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/reference/moonbase-phases/)**[\[13\]](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/04/260425123456.htm)** CLPS task orders cover a diversity of payloads: resource prospecting (e.g., the cancelled‑then‑revived VIPER rover planned to map south‑pole ice), drilling demonstrations (PRIME‑1), dust‑mitigation technology tests, and mobility experiments.[**\[20\]**](https://www.planetary.org/space-missions/viper)**[\[21\]](https://www.nasa.gov/mission/polar-resources-ice-mining-experiment-1-prime-1/)**

Dependencies: launchers, commercial landers, DSN/relay communications, power at lander scale, and robust autonomy.

Delays / failures: CLPS missions have seen substantial overruns and partial failures; PRIME‑1 appears to have operated only briefly after landing, and VIPER was cancelled once due to budget concerns.[**\[9\]**](https://oig.nasa.gov/docs/IG-24-011.pdf)**[\[20\]](https://www.planetary.org/space-missions/viper)[\[21\]](https://www.nasa.gov/mission/polar-resources-ice-mining-experiment-1-prime-1/)** Gamewise, this supports risk of partial data or lost payloads even when the launch succeeds.

**Game objective hook:** Survey missions unlock:

* Site‑specific knowledge (e.g., “high likelihood of water ice in this PSR rim area”).  
* Incremental TRL gains for technologies (e.g., dust mitigation, drilling, mobility).  
* Confidence metrics for future crewed‑mission risk at that region.

### **2.4 Lander Development and Test**

**Purpose‑built lunar landers must be flight‑tested before crewed operations or heavy‑cargo reliance.** Historically, Apollo’s Lunar Module flew in Earth orbit (Apollo 5, 9\) before lunar use.[**\[22\]**](https://history.nasa.gov/afj/ap09fj/01intro.html) Artemis uses commercial human landing systems (HLS) that are new architectures with major schedule and integration risks; NASA’s Inspector General has flagged both providers as experiencing delays and safety concerns.[**\[11\]**](https://oig.nasa.gov/news/artemis-lander-program-faces-schedule-delays-and-unmitigated-crew-safety-risks/)

Current CLPS and Moon Base cargo landers (e.g., Blue Moon Mark 1, Griffin) are undergoing thermal‑vacuum, vibration, and integrated systems tests.[**\[23\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/blue-moon-mark-1-thermal-vacuum-testing/) These activities are classic programme‑management bottlenecks: slipped environmental tests or design flaws delay everything that depends on that lander family.

**Game objective hook:** The player funds lander families with attributes (payload, precision landing, hazard‑avoidance sensors, reliability). Before these reach “operational” status, they must survive a sequence of test flights; failures cost time and budget and may force re‑architecting of surface logisitics.

### **2.5 Delivery of Cargo, Power and Communications Infrastructure**

**Early cargo flights pre‑position power, communications, and mobility before crew.** NASA’s architecture identifies initial power at “tens of kilowatts” with grid‑like distribution, likely starting with solar photovoltaic plus energy storage and later adding fission reactors.[**\[24\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2542435122000761)**[\[25\]](https://www.energy.gov/ne/articles/nasa-and-doe-partner-develop-nuclear-power-moon-and-mars)** Studies emphasise that batteries alone to ride out a 354‑hour lunar night for a modest 10 kW habitat become very challenging, hence interest in regenerative fuel cells (RFCs), nuclear fission surface power (e.g., the planned Lunar Reactor‑1 \>20 kWe in \~2030), and power‑beaming concepts.[**\[24\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2542435122000761)**[\[25\]](https://www.energy.gov/ne/articles/nasa-and-doe-partner-develop-nuclear-power-moon-and-mars)[\[26\]](https://www.nasa.gov/general/nasa-regenerative-fuel-cell-testing/)[\[27\]](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44453-026-00053-w)**

On communications, NASA’s LunaNet / Lunar Communications Relay and Navigation Services (LCRNS) plan constellations of relay satellites to provide continuous coverage for south‑pole and far‑side users. A single relay offers \~41% south‑pole coverage, whereas constellations (24 satellites in one study; NASA’s baseline is smaller but multi‑satellite) can approach continuous coverage.[**\[8\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/space-communications-and-navigation/lunar-communications-relay-and-navigation-services/)**[\[28\]](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/lunanet-concept.pdf)[\[29\]](https://arc.aiaa.org/doi/10.2514/6.2020-0419)** Initial surface operations rely on a mix of direct‑to‑Earth opportunities and gradually expanding relay services.

Dependencies: cargo lander TRL, DSN ground network, LunaNet/LCRNS deployment, power components.

Delays: launch slips, relay failure, and incompatibility between early surface systems and later grid architectures.

**Game objective hook:**

* Allocate early cargo mass between static solar arrays, experimental towers, batteries/RFCs, and comms towers vs science payloads.  
* Decide whether to rely on direct‑to‑Earth passes (cheaper, but with regular blackouts) or invest in costly relay infrastructure.

### **2.6 Habitats and Life Support**

**Pressurised habitats and robust life support are still gaps in NASA’s architecture.** Functional requirements FN‑H‑101 (short‑duration pressurised surface habitat) and FN‑H‑102 (long‑duration habitat) are listed as unfilled in Moon Base documentation.[**\[3\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/moon-base-architecture-users-guide.pdf) Planned early solutions include:

* A pressurised rover from JAXA serving as the first mobile habitat for two astronauts in Phase II.[**\[30\]**](https://global.jaxa.jp/press/2023/01/20230112-1.html)  
* A surface habitat module with environmental control and life support (ECLSS) for multi‑week to multi‑month stays, requiring nearly regenerative life support beyond \~120 days.[**\[31\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/artemis-iii-mission-concept.pdf)**[\[32\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20200000316)**

ISS experience shows that high water‑recovery ratios and oxygen recycling are necessary for long stays; NASA’s regenerative life support research targets high water and O₂ recovery to make Moon‑base habitation logistically viable.[**\[32\]**](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20200000316) For south‑pole operations, additional challenges include thermal regulation under low‑Sun elevation, dust sealing, and micrometeoroid protection.[**\[33\]**](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/2020500135)**[\[34\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20160013759)**

Dependencies: power infrastructure, logistics cadence (resupply), crewed landers, dust‑mitigation tech.

Delays: under‑performing ECLSS, dust ingress, and radiation‑shielding mass constraints can push back “permanent” habitation.

**Game objective hook:** Habitat projects become available only after player has:

* Demonstrated sufficient power (e.g., grid capacity threshold).  
* Achieved life‑support TRL via orbital and robotic tests.  
* Established minimum comms uptime.

Crew missions then test these habitats; partial failures may degrade capability (e.g., habitat usable only for short sorties).

### **2.7 ISRU, Resources and Construction**

**ISRU (in‑situ resource utilisation) is a long‑term enabler, not a near‑term prerequisite, and is currently low‑to‑mid TRL.** NASA’s Lunar Surface Innovation Initiative is developing resource‑extraction methods (excavation, beneficiation, thermal extraction) for oxygen and water from regolith and icy soils, especially at the poles.[**\[35\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/directorates/stmd/lunar-surface-innovation-initiative/)**[\[36\]](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1742-6596/1543/1/012025)** Laboratory ISRU water‑extraction systems show partial recovery and efficiency but are far from routine operational deployments.[**\[36\]**](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1742-6596/1543/1/012025)

Water‑ice prospecting missions (VIPER, PRIME‑1, PROMISE) demonstrate the riskiness of this domain: VIPER was cancelled in 2024 due to cost; PRIME‑1 appears to have had only brief operations; PROMISE (a nuclear‑powered rover using an MMRTG) is planned for late 2028 to drill \~1 m into PSR‑adjacent soils.[**\[20\]**](https://www.planetary.org/space-missions/viper)**[\[21\]](https://www.nasa.gov/mission/polar-resources-ice-mining-experiment-1-prime-1/)[\[37\]](https://www.nasa.gov/missions/promise-nuclear-powered-lunar-rover/)** Construction using regolith 3D printing remains experimental, with multiple concepts (laser sintering, binder‑based “bricks”, dome structures) being tested at sub‑scale and low TRLs.[**\[38\]**](https://www.mdpi.com/2075-5309/10/11/195)

Dependencies: robust mobility in PSR‑adjacent terrains, drilling and thermal systems, high‑reliability power independent of sunlight (e.g., RTGs, fission, power‑beaming).

Delays: mission failures, under‑performing extraction yields, and contamination or thermal issues in PSRs.

**Game objective hook:** ISRU is an optional but powerful branch:

* Early: send prospectors to raise knowledge of ice/regolith quality and raise ISRU TRL.  
* Mid‑late: invest in demonstration plants that, if successful, reduce imported water/oxygen demand, freeing launch mass for other capabilities.

### **2.8 First Crewed Missions and Expansion**

**Initial Artemis surface missions are short—order of two weeks—before evolving to longer stays.** NASA targets \~14‑day surface missions with two \~2‑hour moonwalks initially, gradually building to missions \>120 days where fully regenerative life support becomes attractive.[**\[31\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/artemis-iii-mission-concept.pdf)**[\[32\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20200000316)** Radiation measurements from recent lunar surface missions indicate daily doses several times ISS levels, implying stringent cumulative dose management for crew career limits.[**\[39\]**](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aba3000)**[\[40\]](https://www.nasa.gov/feature/nasa-s-artemis-i-mission-sets-stage-for-human-return-to-moon)[\[41\]](https://standards.nasa.gov/standard/nasa/nasa-std-3001-vol-1)**

Dependencies: human‑rated lander, suits (e.g., AxEMU), proven ECLSS, surface mobility (LTVs), and emergency shelters.

Delays: spacesuit development has already been flagged as at risk relative to landing dates; risk‑management panels have called some Artemis timelines “high risk”.[**\[42\]**](https://oiir.hq.nasa.gov/asap/documents/2024_ASAP_Annual_Report.pdf)**[\[43\]](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-22-105195)**

**Game objective hook:** Initial crewed sorties:

* Validate habitats and power systems under load.  
* Unlock new research categories (in‑situ geology, complex ISRU experiments).  
* Carry heavy programme consequences for crew loss or major incident (e.g., budget cuts, public‑support penalty, forced “safer” timeline).

### **2.9 Long‑Term Sustainable Operations**

**True sustainability requires closing several loops and achieving a robust logistics cadence.** NASA’s Moon Base Phase III envisions:

* Permanent or near‑permanent habitats with thick radiation and micrometeoroid shielding (possibly using regolith berms or partially buried structures).[**\[2\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/lunar/strategies/resources/M2M_ACR2025_WhyMoonAndMars_v2.pdf)**[\[33\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/2020500135)**  
* Fission reactors (e.g., LR‑1) for continuous power through polar night, integrated with distributed solar arrays and grids.[**\[25\]**](https://www.energy.gov/ne/articles/nasa-and-doe-partner-develop-nuclear-power-moon-and-mars)**[\[26\]](https://www.nasa.gov/general/nasa-regenerative-fuel-cell-testing/)[\[27\]](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44453-026-00053-w)**  
* Operational ISRU producing a fraction of water, oxygen, and possibly propellant.[**\[35\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/directorates/stmd/lunar-surface-innovation-initiative/)**[\[36\]](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1742-6596/1543/1/012025)**  
* Mature transportation infrastructure (LTVs, pressurised rovers, regular CLPS cargo).

Dependencies: all earlier phases plus sufficient political and economic support to sustain high‑cadence launches.

For Stargazer, the “colony” endgame should be defined not as a visual sprawl but as meeting quantifiable sustainability criteria (section 7).

**3Part 3 — Real Engineering Challenges (with Game Hooks)**

| Challenge | Real‑world explanation | Example | Engineering response | Game opportunity |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Polar illumination vs darkness | South‑pole terrain yields areas with 70–94% annual sunlight on peaks, while nearby craters are permanently shadowed; global day/night cycle \~29.5 days.[**\[4\]**](https://www.planetary.org/space-images/shackleton-crater-illumination)**[\[7\]](https://www.nasa.gov/reference/moonbase-environment/)[\[17\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0032063318302421)** | Peaks near Shackleton Crater illuminated \~94% of a lunar year.[**\[4\]**](https://www.planetary.org/space-images/shackleton-crater-illumination) | Optimise placement of solar arrays; combine PV with storage, fission, or power‑beaming to survive dark periods.[**\[24\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2542435122000761)**[\[25\]](https://www.energy.gov/ne/articles/nasa-and-doe-partner-develop-nuclear-power-moon-and-mars)[\[27\]](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44453-026-00053-w)** | Use Stargazer DEM/horizon engine to pick power sites; mis‑chosen sites force costly storage or night‑time curtailment. |
| Lunar night energy storage | A 10 kW habitat consumes many MWh over a 354‑hour night; batteries alone become massive and costly.[**\[24\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2542435122000761) | Studies highlight difficulty of battery‑only survival through lunar night for kilowatt‑class loads.[**\[24\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2542435122000761) | RFCs, fission reactors, and possibly beamed power supplement PV.[**\[24\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2542435122000761)**[\[25\]](https://www.energy.gov/ne/articles/nasa-and-doe-partner-develop-nuclear-power-moon-and-mars)[\[26\]](https://www.nasa.gov/general/nasa-regenerative-fuel-cell-testing/)[\[27\]](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44453-026-00053-w)** | Decide when to unlock and invest in advanced storage or fission vs expanding solar; wrong timing leads to brownouts or aborted missions. |
| Communications geometry | South‑pole sites have direct Earth view for only \~half of each synodic month, and Earth‑visibility windows do not align neatly with sunlight periods.[**\[5\]**](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2018JE005668)**[\[6\]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/319406298_Visibility_and_Lighting_Conditions_on_a_Modelled_Lunar_Surface)[\[7\]](https://www.nasa.gov/reference/moonbase-environment/)** | Studies show \~14 days of Earth visibility per lunar month at many south‑pole sites.[**\[5\]**](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2018JE005668) | Relay constellations (LunaNet/LCRNS) and Gateway‑like relays; onboard buffering for blackouts.[**\[8\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/space-communications-and-navigation/lunar-communications-relay-and-navigation-services/)**[\[28\]](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/lunanet-concept.pdf)[\[29\]](https://arc.aiaa.org/doi/10.2514/6.2020-0419)** | Player chooses whether to accept long blackouts (cheaper) or pay for relays; blackout episodes risk data loss or heightened crew hazard. |
| Signal delay vs blackout | One‑way light‑time \~1.3 s; planned blackouts \~40 min when spacecraft passes behind Moon.[**\[28\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/lunanet-concept.pdf)**[\[44\]](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/artemis-ii-reference-guide.pdf)[\[45\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20230002268)** | Artemis‑class Orion experiences \~41 min comms blackout behind the Moon.[**\[44\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/artemis-ii-reference-guide.pdf) | Autonomy for critical phases; procedures tuned for delayed ground control.[**\[44\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/artemis-ii-reference-guide.pdf)**[\[46\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20230002268)** | Educate by separating “lag” (affects tele‑ops) from total loss; in missions, players must pre‑plan autonomous actions for blackout intervals. |
| Landing safety in rough terrain | South pole is heavily cratered; safe landing requires low slopes (goal ≤5–8°), avoidance of boulders and fresh craters, and hazard‑detection sensors.[**\[14\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/lro/lola/)**[\[15\]](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/17/9/1579)[\[16\]](https://aerospaceamerica.aiaa.org/features/the-choice/)** | Artemis landing‑site criteria specify slope thresholds and boulder avoidance distances.[**\[15\]**](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/17/9/1579)**[\[16\]](https://aerospaceamerica.aiaa.org/features/the-choice/)** | Precision navigation, hazard‑avoidance lidar/cameras, thorough DEM‑based screening.[**\[14\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/lro/lola/)**[\[15\]](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/17/9/1579)** | Site‑selection UI highlights hazard metrics; pushing for “science‑rich” but rough terrain increases landing‑failure risk. |
| Dust | Lunar dust is abrasive, electrostatically clings to surfaces, degrades thermal control, and caused respiratory symptoms in Apollo crew.[**\[47\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/science-research/science-at-nasa/2005/30aug_lunardust/)**[\[48\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0032063317300252)** | Apollo astronauts reported sneezing; dust scratched visors and suit layers.[**\[47\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/science-research/science-at-nasa/2005/30aug_lunardust/)**[\[49\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19720002945)** | Dust‑tolerant fabrics, electrodynamic shields, passive coatings, operational protocols.[**\[47\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/science-research/science-at-nasa/2005/30aug_lunardust/)**[\[50\]](https://www.nasa.gov/centers-and-facilities/johnson/eds-lunar-dust-mitigation/)** | Missions accumulate “dust burden” on assets; invest in mitigation tech to keep solar arrays and radiators effective. |
| Radiation | Lunar surface radiation is \~hundreds of times Earth background and several‑fold ISS levels; cumulative exposure constrained by NASA career limits (\~600 mSv).[**\[39\]**](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aba3000)**[\[40\]](https://www.nasa.gov/feature/nasa-s-artemis-i-mission-sets-stage-for-human-return-to-moon)[\[41\]](https://standards.nasa.gov/standard/nasa/nasa-std-3001-vol-1)** | Lunar surface dosimetry indicates \~2–3× ISS daily dose.[**\[40\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/feature/nasa-s-artemis-i-mission-sets-stage-for-human-return-to-moon)**[\[41\]](https://standards.nasa.gov/standard/nasa/nasa-std-3001-vol-1)** | Shielding (regolith berms, water), time‑limited stays, operational constraints during solar events.[**\[33\]**](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/2020500135)**[\[39\]](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aba3000)** | Long missions increase crew‑dose gauge; player must improve shielding or accept shorter stays and rotation overhead. |
| Micrometeoroids | No atmosphere to burn up debris; small impacts threaten equipment and unshielded structures.[**\[33\]**](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/2020500135)**[\[51\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20140008007)** | NASA uses Meteoroid Engineering Models to assess south‑pole hazard.[**\[51\]**](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20140008007) | Whipple shields, burying tanks/pipes, selecting sheltered sites.[**\[33\]**](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/2020500135)**[\[51\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20140008007)** | Location choice modifies background failure rate; investing in protective works reduces random “impact” events. |
| Life support closure | Long‑duration stays require high water/O₂ recycling; systems are complex and sensitive.[**\[32\]**](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20200000316) | ISS regenerative ECLSS milestones show slow progress to high recovery.[**\[32\]**](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20200000316) | Incremental tech maturation via ISS and analogues; redundancy and repair capability.[**\[31\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/artemis-iii-mission-concept.pdf)**[\[32\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20200000316)** | Research tree: partial closure reduces resupply mass; pushing immature systems too early risks failures on‑surface. |
| ISRU uncertainty | Abundances, form, and accessibility of polar ice are poorly constrained; extraction TRL is low.[**\[35\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/directorates/stmd/lunar-surface-innovation-initiative/)**[\[36\]](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1742-6596/1543/1/012025)** | VIPER cancellation and PRIME‑1’s short lifetime illustrate risk of early resource prospecting.[**\[20\]**](https://www.planetary.org/space-missions/viper)**[\[21\]](https://www.nasa.gov/mission/polar-resources-ice-mining-experiment-1-prime-1/)** | Multi‑mission prospecting, conservative incorporation into logistics until demonstrated.[**\[35\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/directorates/stmd/lunar-surface-innovation-initiative/)**[\[36\]](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1742-6596/1543/1/012025)** | High‑risk / high‑reward branch: early over‑commitment to ISRU can backfire if missions fail or resource is sparse. |
| Launch windows & weather | Earth launches must hit narrow windows (few hours) that shift \~40 minutes per day, and are constrained by complex weather “commit criteria”.[**\[52\]**](https://blogs.nasa.gov/artemis/2026/03/29/artemis-ii-launch-windows/)**[\[53\]](https://www.nasa.gov/feature/launch-weather-criteria/)[\[54\]](https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/artemis-ii-lcc-fact-sheet.pdf)** | Artemis II had two‑hour launch windows that shift daily; thick cumulus clouds and high winds are no‑go conditions.[**\[52\]**](https://blogs.nasa.gov/artemis/2026/03/29/artemis-ii-launch-windows/)**[\[53\]](https://www.nasa.gov/feature/launch-weather-criteria/)[\[54\]](https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/artemis-ii-lcc-fact-sheet.pdf)** | Flexible range scheduling, scrub/recycle procedures, backup windows each month.[**\[52\]**](https://blogs.nasa.gov/artemis/2026/03/29/artemis-ii-launch-windows/)**[\[53\]](https://www.nasa.gov/feature/launch-weather-criteria/)** | Strategic choice: aim for earliest window (higher risk of scrub) vs later, more favourable but pushes arrival into less optimal polar lighting. |
| Programme cost & delay | Artemis/CLPS exhibit schedule slips and cost overruns; CLPS averaged \~26% cost overrun and 14‑month delay per task order.[**\[9\]**](https://oig.nasa.gov/docs/IG-24-011.pdf)**[\[10\]](https://oig.nasa.gov/docs/IG-23-003.pdf)[\[11\]](https://oig.nasa.gov/news/artemis-lander-program-faces-schedule-delays-and-unmitigated-crew-safety-risks/)** | Artemis missions repeatedly delayed due to rocket, lander, and spacesuit issues.[**\[11\]**](https://oig.nasa.gov/news/artemis-lander-program-faces-schedule-delays-and-unmitigated-crew-safety-risks/)**[\[42\]](https://oiir.hq.nasa.gov/asap/documents/2024_ASAP_Annual_Report.pdf)[\[43\]](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-22-105195)** | Incremental milestones, diversified providers, robust systems engineering & PRA.[**\[11\]**](https://oig.nasa.gov/news/artemis-lander-program-faces-schedule-delays-and-unmitigated-crew-safety-risks/)**[\[55\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20210025751)** | Meta‑game: overruns shrink future budgets and slip critical path; player hedges with parallel developments or lower‑risk options. |

---

**4Part 4 — Programme Management Challenges**

**Lunar exploration architectures are governed as large, interdependent portfolios, not as sequences of independent missions.** Apollo’s success was often described as a triumph of programme management and systems engineering, coordinating thousands of contractors and complex hardware under tight timelines.[**\[56\]**](https://history.nasa.gov/SP-4102.pdf) Modern Artemis/Moon Base programmes inherit similar complexity but with added commercial diversity and budget volatility.

### **4.1 Budget and Portfolio Constraints**

Artemis is a multi‑tens‑of‑billions‑dollar programme through the mid‑2020s, with per‑launch costs in the billions and documented overruns across major projects.[**\[10\]**](https://oig.nasa.gov/docs/IG-23-003.pdf)**[\[11\]](https://oig.nasa.gov/news/artemis-lander-program-faces-schedule-delays-and-unmitigated-crew-safety-risks/)** CLPS is an IDIQ contract mechanism with a nominal \$2.6B ceiling through 2028,[**\[57\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/commercial-lunar-payload-services/) but individual task orders have substantially grown beyond original values.[**\[9\]**](https://oig.nasa.gov/docs/IG-24-011.pdf) In practice, this means:

* Not every desirable precursor mission or technology can be funded.  
* Failures or overruns in one element (e.g., lander, suits) can cannibalise funds from others.

In game terms, “budget” should not be a simple currency, but a capacity to run parallel development lines; overruns lock those slots longer and shrink future discretionary capital.

### **4.2 Development Timelines and TRL**

NASA uses Technology Readiness Levels (1–9) to track maturation of components and systems, with TRL 7–9 representing system‑level demonstration in relevant or operational environments.[**\[12\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/trl.pdf) NextSTEP, LSII and related technology programmes aim to push power, mobility, ISRU, and life‑support technologies into TRL 5–6 before committing them to mission‑critical roles.[**\[31\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/artemis-iii-mission-concept.pdf)**[\[35\]](https://www.nasa.gov/directorates/stmd/lunar-surface-innovation-initiative/)**

A realistic dependency chain:

* Subsystem at TRL 3–4 → lab breadboard; cannot be used on critical missions.  
* TRL 5–6 → tested in relevant environment (e.g., robotic demonstration).  
* TRL 7–8 → flown on operational mission; becomes viable baseline for crewed or base‑critical systems.

In game, each mission can raise TRL for certain tech; base‑critical deployments require prior demonstrations. This enforces meaningful sequencing: you cannot base your primary power grid on an unflown innovative array.

### **4.3 Launch, Transit and Arrival Scheduling**

Launch windows are a key synchronisation constraint:

* **Earth launch windows:** For Artemis‑class missions, daily windows of \~2 hours, shifting \~40 min per day, constrained by Earth‑Moon geometry, orbital mechanics, reentry lighting, and thermal limits.[**\[52\]**](https://blogs.nasa.gov/artemis/2026/03/29/artemis-ii-launch-windows/)**[\[58\]](https://arc.aiaa.org/doi/10.2514/6.2019-0920)**  
* **Monthly launch periods:** Multi‑day sequences when trans‑lunar injection is feasible with acceptable performance.[**\[58\]**](https://arc.aiaa.org/doi/10.2514/6.2019-0920)

On top of this, launch‑site weather imposes a large set of “launch commit criteria”—winds, icing, clouds (especially thick cumulus to avoid triggered lightning), upper‑air temperatures—resulting in scrubs even when hardware is ready.[**\[53\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/feature/launch-weather-criteria/)**[\[54\]](https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/artemis-ii-lcc-fact-sheet.pdf)**

Crucially, **Earth launch windows and lunar surface conditions are only loosely coupled.** A slip of a few days can rotate a desired south‑pole arrival from a period of long continuous sunlight into one with fragmented illumination, or mis‑align Earth visibility phases. This is exactly where Stargazer’s engine is valuable: given a selected landing region, it can show how arrival date shifts change the illumination/Earth‑visibility timeline.

### **4.4 Astronaut Training and Crew Availability**

Astronaut candidates undergo \~two years of basic training, plus mission‑specific training for each flight; Artemis surface crews also train in multiple terrestrial analog sites to practice geology and EVA skills.[**\[59\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/features/2024/020924/preparing-for-artemis/)**[\[60\]](https://astronomy.com/news/2026/03/nasa-unveils-ambitious-moon-base-plan)** Career radiation limits and operational constraints restrict how many long‑duration lunar missions each astronaut can fly.[**\[39\]**](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aba3000)**[\[41\]](https://standards.nasa.gov/standard/nasa/nasa-std-3001-vol-1)**

Programme implications:

* Crew assignments are long‑lead decisions; a mission delay might push a trained crew into schedule conflict with other roles.  
* High radiation dose on a long‑duration mission may effectively “use up” a significant portion of a crew member’s career dose budget.

A simplified game abstraction: limited “experienced crew slots” that recharge slowly; sending them on hazardous missions reduces their future availability.

### **4.5 Inter‑Project Dependencies and Cascading Delays**

Real examples of dependencies:

* HLS lander readiness is a critical path for Artemis III and later surface missions; schedule slips in Starship or Blue Moon ripple directly into base timelines.[**\[11\]**](https://oig.nasa.gov/news/artemis-lander-program-faces-schedule-delays-and-unmitigated-crew-safety-risks/)  
* Spacesuit (AxEMU) delays have been flagged as potential blockers for landing dates.[**\[42\]**](https://oiir.hq.nasa.gov/asap/documents/2024_ASAP_Annual_Report.pdf)**[\[43\]](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-22-105195)**  
* VIPER cancellation removed a planned source of high‑fidelity water‑ice maps, increasing uncertainty for ISRU‑dependent architectures.[**\[20\]**](https://www.planetary.org/space-missions/viper)

Mechanistically, dependencies look like directed graphs: a habitat mission requires (lander family A at TRL 9\) AND (AxEMU at TRL 8–9) AND (power system P at TRL 7+). A delay in any upstream node forces re‑planning.

Gamewise, this motivates a UI emphasising **critical path management**: the player can see which future capability (e.g., “Crewed 60‑day stay”) is gated by which chain of developments, and can choose to:

* Fund risk‑reduction tests to shorten that path.  
* De‑scope certain missions to reduce dependence on a high‑risk technology.

---

**5Part 5 — Historical and Modern Mission Lessons**

### **5.1 Apollo**

* **Objectives:** Beat the geopolitical schedule, perform initial surface exploration and sample return.  
* **Engineering challenges:** Precision landing without atmospheric braking; LM design; on‑orbit rendezvous; limited surface stay with portable life support.  
* **Decisions and constraints:** Landing‑site safety dominated early choices; Apollo 11 targeted relatively flat mare terrain with minimal hazards.[**\[61\]**](https://history.nasa.gov/SP-287/ch2.htm)  
* **Achievements:** Demonstrated crewed landings, short EVAs, sample collection, and LM ascent/descent under tight margins.  
* **Unresolved for long‑term colonies:** Regenerative life support, dust mitigation (dust significantly degraded systems and affected crew), long‑duration radiation exposure, and robust surface logistics were not solved.[**\[47\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/science-research/science-at-nasa/2005/30aug_lunardust/)**[\[49\]](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19720002945)**

Gameplay lesson: Use Apollo‑style missions as “tutorials” on fuel margins, landing hazards, and mission‑control coordination, but emphasise that these are **short sorties**, not colonisation.

### **5.2 Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) and LOLA**

* **Objectives:** Map lunar topography, illumination, temperatures, and potential volatiles, especially at the poles.[**\[14\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/lro/lola/)**[\[18\]](https://science.nasa.gov/science-research/science-at-nasa/2006/06nov_moonwater/)**  
* **Challenges:** High‑resolution polar mapping, orbit design for persistent coverage, instrument calibration.  
* **Achievements:** Detailed DEMs, illumination maps, PSR identification, and environmental data became foundational to Artemis site planning.[**\[14\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/lro/lola/)**[\[18\]](https://science.nasa.gov/science-research/science-at-nasa/2006/06nov_moonwater/)**  
* **Lesson:** High‑fidelity mapping drastically reduces risk for later stages.

Gameplay lesson: Orbital reconnaissance missions become early‑tree activities that unlock site‑selection overlays and reduce uncertainty in hazard and illumination assessments.

### **5.3 Artemis Programme**

* **Objectives:** Return humans to the Moon, then establish a sustained south‑pole presence integrated into a Moon‑to‑Mars architecture.[**\[2\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/lunar/strategies/resources/M2M_ACR2025_WhyMoonAndMars_v2.pdf)**[\[31\]](https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/artemis-iii-mission-concept.pdf)**  
* **Challenges:** New SLS/Orion hardware, new commercial HLS, new suits, and new surface infrastructure; significant integration complexity.  
* **Constraints and delays:** Multiple Artemis missions have slipped years due to technical issues (e.g., hydrogen leaks, heat shield issues, HLS delays, suit development).[**\[11\]**](https://oig.nasa.gov/news/artemis-lander-program-faces-schedule-delays-and-unmitigated-crew-safety-risks/)**[\[42\]](https://oiir.hq.nasa.gov/asap/documents/2024_ASAP_Annual_Report.pdf)[\[43\]](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-22-105195)**  
* **Architecture:** Phased, with many robotic missions, initial short‑duration surface stays, pressurised rover/habitats in Phase II, and later ISRU and fission power in Phase III.[**\[1\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/reference/moonbase-phases/)**[\[2\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/lunar/strategies/resources/M2M_ACR2025_WhyMoonAndMars_v2.pdf)[\[3\]](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/moon-base-architecture-users-guide.pdf)[\[30\]](https://global.jaxa.jp/press/2023/01/20230112-1.html)**

Gameplay lesson: Delay and re‑scoping are **normal**; players should be rewarded for robust architectures that can absorb shifts rather than punished only by binary “mission failed”.

### **5.4 CLPS and Other Robotic Landers**

* **Objectives:** Provide rapid, commercial payload delivery to the Moon for science and tech demos.[**\[57\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/commercial-lunar-payload-services/)  
* **Challenges:** New lander designs, commercial risk tolerance, mixed maturity levels; first commercial lunar landings saw partial successes and failures.  
* **Achievements:** Demonstrated commercial sea‑change in delivery mechanisms but with significant schedule slips and overruns.[**\[9\]**](https://oig.nasa.gov/docs/IG-24-011.pdf)**[\[10\]](https://oig.nasa.gov/docs/IG-23-003.pdf)**  
* **Unresolved:** How to achieve airline‑like regularity and reliability in cis‑lunar logistics.

Gameplay lesson: Represent CLPS‑like services as a stochastic but flexible logistics channel; players can pay a premium for higher reliability or accept cheaper providers with higher risk and possible overruns.

### **5.5 Prospective Moon Base Architectures**

NASA’s Moon Base documents and related architecture studies provide a rich set of:

* Functional requirements for power, habitats, mobility, logistics, and science.[**\[3\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/moon-base-architecture-users-guide.pdf)**[\[24\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2542435122000761)[\[59\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/features/2024/020924/preparing-for-artemis/)**  
* Phase‑by‑phase payload, launch, and capability build‑up (e.g., dozens of launches and tens of tonnes of cargo over Phase II).[**\[2\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/lunar/strategies/resources/M2M_ACR2025_WhyMoonAndMars_v2.pdf)**[\[60\]](https://astronomy.com/news/2026/03/nasa-unveils-ambitious-moon-base-plan)**  
* Explicit notation of gaps: habitats, advanced power, some ISRU are still to be filled.

Gameplay lesson: Ground the research tree directly in these functional categories: when the document lists “Generate power at south pole” and “Enable pressurised habitat for long durations” as distinct functions, these become explicit capability milestones in the game.

**6Part 6 — Gameplay Conflicts**

| Player decision | Benefit | Sacrifice or risk | Long‑term consequence | Real‑world basis |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Launch early vs wait for better polar lighting | Earlier science/infrastructure, political momentum. | Higher risk of unfavourable illumination/Earth visibility; more complex power/comms operations. | May lock architecture into suboptimal base layout or require costly retrofits. | South‑pole lighting/Earth visibility vary with date; launch windows may not align with ideal site conditions.[**\[4\]**](https://www.planetary.org/space-images/shackleton-crater-illumination)**[\[5\]](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2018JE005668)[\[7\]](https://www.nasa.gov/reference/moonbase-environment/)[\[52\]](https://blogs.nasa.gov/artemis/2026/03/29/artemis-ii-launch-windows/)** |
| Invest heavily in solar \+ storage vs accelerate fission power | Lower political risk, uses mature PV tech; simpler early missions. | Large mass to batteries/RFCs; struggles with long dark periods; later “big bang” cost to switch architectures. | Early solar focus may slow ability to support long stays in PSRs or through winter seasons. | NASA traded PV‑storage vs fission; plans to deploy fission surface power (\~2030) recognising PV limits.[**\[24\]**](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2542435122000761)**[\[25\]](https://www.energy.gov/ne/articles/nasa-and-doe-partner-develop-nuclear-power-moon-and-mars)[\[26\]](https://www.nasa.gov/general/nasa-regenerative-fuel-cell-testing/)[\[27\]](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44453-026-00053-w)** |
| Rely on direct‑to‑Earth passes vs fund relay satellites | Avoids high upfront satellite costs; simpler ops. | Regular blackouts at south pole; limits location choices to high‑Earth‑visibility ridges. | May preclude expansion into PSRs and far‑side‑like regions; later retrofits are disruptive. | LunaNet/LCRNS architectures designed because south‑pole sites cannot maintain continuous direct Earth view.[**\[5\]**](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2018JE005668)**[\[8\]](https://www.nasa.gov/space-communications-and-navigation/lunar-communications-relay-and-navigation-services/)[\[28\]](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/lunanet-concept.pdf)[\[29\]](https://arc.aiaa.org/doi/10.2514/6.2020-0419)** |
| Heavy early resource‑prospecting vs focus on immediate base needs | Early ISRU knowledge could dramatically cut future logistics mass. | High risk of robotic mission failure; consumes launch and budget that could fund power/habitat infrastructure. | If ISRU fails or ice is sparse, early focus leaves base underpowered/undersupplied; if it succeeds, long‑term logistics are transformed. | VIPER cancellation and PRIME‑1 risks highlight uncertainty and programme‑level trade‑offs in ISRU investments.[**\[20\]**](https://www.planetary.org/space-missions/viper)**[\[21\]](https://www.nasa.gov/mission/polar-resources-ice-mining-experiment-1-prime-1/)[\[35\]](https://www.nasa.gov/directorates/stmd/lunar-surface-innovation-initiative/)[\[36\]](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1742-6596/1543/1/012025)** |
| Aggressive schedule with low TRL systems vs conservative phased adoption | Faster path to “colony”; headline achievements. | Higher mission‑failure risk; cascading schedule slips if unproven tech fails. | Could lead to high‑profile accidents → political backlash, budget cuts; or, if lucky, leapfrog capabilities. | Artemis safety panels warning about HLS and suit readiness; TRL framework emphasises staged maturation.[**\[11\]**](https://oig.nasa.gov/news/artemis-lander-program-faces-schedule-delays-and-unmitigated-crew-safety-risks/)**[\[12\]](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/trl.pdf)[\[42\]](https://oiir.hq.nasa.gov/asap/documents/2024_ASAP_Annual_Report.pdf)[\[43\]](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-22-105195)** |
| Large early habitat vs incremental, sortie‑first approach | Immediate visible “base”; ability to host long missions sooner. | Massive initial cost and risk; habitat idle if power/comms/logistics lag. | If successful, accelerates sustainability; if not, becomes stranded asset. | Moon Base plan emphasises pressurised rover and small surface habitat first, with larger infrastructure later.[**\[2\]**](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/lunar/strategies/resources/M2M_ACR2025_WhyMoonAndMars_v2.pdf)**[\[3\]](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/moon-base-architecture-users-guide.pdf)[\[30\]](https://global.jaxa.jp/press/2023/01/20230112-1.html)[\[59\]](https://www.lpi.usra.edu/features/2024/020924/preparing-for-artemis/)** |
| More crew vs more robots | Human flexibility and high scientific return. | Higher life‑support mass, radiation risk, cost per mission; complex training pipeline. | Faster science/ops but greater exposure to crises; may crowd out robotic tech demos. | Artemis balances crewed missions with many robotic CLPS missions; ISS experience shows cost of crew presence.[**\[1\]**](https://www.nasa.gov/reference/moonbase-phases/)**[\[31\]](https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/artemis-iii-mission-concept.pdf)[\[57\]](https://www.nasa.gov/commercial-lunar-payload-services/)** |
| Concentrate base near PSRs vs on better‑lit ridges | Access to potential water ice; compelling science. | Dark, cold, comms‑challenged environment; heavier dependence on alternative power. | Long‑term advantage if ISRU succeeds; near‑term complexity and risk. | South‑pole PSRs near Shackleton host potential ice but are permanently shadowed and extremely cold.[**\[18\]**](https://science.nasa.gov/science-research/science-at-nasa/2006/06nov_moonwater/)**[\[19\]](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-020-01222-x)** |
| Choose high‑reliability commercial providers vs cheapest | Fewer delays and failures; predictable logistics. | Higher per‑mission cost; lower mission count for same budget. | Smoother architecture execution vs slower capability expansion. | CLPS cost/delay statistics vary by provider; NASA spreads risk across multiple vendors.[**\[9\]**](https://oig.nasa.gov/docs/IG-24-011.pdf)**[\[10\]](https://oig.nasa.gov/docs/IG-23-003.pdf)[\[57\]](https://www.nasa.gov/commercial-lunar-payload-services/)** |

Each conflict can be simplified by:

* Representing risk probabilistically with clear feedback (“High‑risk choice: \+X% failure chance, −Y years to capability if successful”).  
* Compressing timescales (e.g., 1 in‑game month \= several real months) but preserving ordering (survey → demo → operational).  
* Abstracting cost into a small number of resource pools (budget, launch capacity, political capital).

---

**7Part 7 — Colony Progression and Research System**

A scientifically grounded progression system should distinguish:

* **Knowledge** (maps, environmental data, resource characterisation).  
* **Technology** (TRL of subsystems).  
* **Infrastructure** (installed hardware on/around Moon).  
* **Operational capability** (what missions can be executed at what risk).  
* **Sustainability** (degree of dependence on Earth resupply and operational margins).

### **7.1 Proposed Research & Capability Categories**

1. **Lunar Mapping & Environment**  
   * Unlocks: terrain maps, DEM quality levels, illumination and Earth‑vis overlays, hazard probabilistic models.  
   * Milestones: global mapping, regional high‑res mapping, site‑specific hazard maps.  
2. **Power & Energy**  
   * PV arrays, masts/towers (e.g., “power towers”), energy storage (batteries, RFCs), fission reactors, beamed power.  
   * Milestones: base‑level power capacity tiers (e.g., “sustain N kW through night”) that gate habitat size, number of concurrent assets.  
3. **Communications & Navigation**  
   * Direct‑to‑Earth systems, relay satellites, LunaNet compatibility, local surface networks.  
   * Milestones: comms uptime percentages at key sites (e.g., 50%, 90%, 99%+), PNT precision enabling autonomous rovers.  
4. **Transportation & Landing Systems**  
   * Lander families, ascent vehicles, orbital tugs, LTV rovers.  
   * Milestones: reliable cargo landings, crewed landing, precision landing within X m, regular resupply cadence.  
5. **Habitats & Life Support**  
   * Pressurised rover, short‑duration habitat, long‑duration habitat, ECLSS closure levels.  
   * Milestones: maximum safe crew‑days per year, maximum single‑mission duration.  
6. **Resources & ISRU**  
   * Prospecting tools, extraction plants, processing/refining, storage.  
   * Milestones: percentage of water/O₂ supplied in situ; ability to refuel ascent vehicles.  
7. **Human Operations & Health**  
   * Suits, EVA tools, dust and radiation mitigation, operational protocols.  
   * Milestones: EVA hours per mission, crew safety metrics, psychological support systems.  
8. **Scientific Research**  
   * Geology, volatiles, astrophysics, technology experiments.  
   * Milestones: completion of defined science campaigns; these contribute to victory but are **not** the sole objective.

### **7.2 Measuring Progress Toward a Functioning Colony**

Rather than a flat “100% research completion”, define **colony viability metrics**:

* **Survival autonomy:** Percentage of critical consumables (power, water, oxygen) that can be maintained locally for a reference crew over a reference duration (e.g., 6 months).  
* **Operational resilience:** Ability to tolerate failures: number of simultaneous subsystem failures that can be survived without crew loss (with some time to repair).  
* **Logistical dependence:** Frequency and mass of required resupply launches per year to sustain target operations.  
* **Knowledge completeness:** Mapping and hazard‑model coverage for the base region and logistics routes.

Victory conditions could require:

* Achieving specified thresholds in autonomy and resilience (e.g., “Support a crew of 4 for 180 days with ≤N cargo launches/year and with the ability to survive loss of one major power asset without evacuation”) **and**  
* Completing a core science campaign (e.g., mapping water‑ice distribution to a given uncertainty threshold).

Players cannot reach 100% merely by launching many missions; each mission must:

* Contribute to raising TRL of key systems,  
* Install infrastructure, or  
* Complete a definable knowledge objective.

---

**8Part 8 — Compare Three Game Structures**

### **Option 1 — Lunar Colony Manager (Pure Programme Layer)**

* **Gameplay depth:** Strong in macro‑strategy (budgets, timelines, tech trees, site selection), but limited moment‑to‑moment engagement. Risk of feeling like a spreadsheet.  
* **Educational value:** Good for conveying dependencies, TRL, and portfolio management; weaker at conveying local terrain/visibility realities.  
* **Scientific credibility:** High if grounded in real architectures and constraints; easier to keep approximate rather than physically precise.  
* **Technical complexity:** Moderate; primarily systems/UX work, minimal real‑time 3D beyond map visualisation.  
* **Reusability of existing engine:** Underused. Stargazer’s high‑fidelity 3D terrain and horizon calculations would be mostly reduced to static overlays.  
* **Suitability for teachers/public:** Teachers may appreciate the planning model, but students may find it abstract.

### **Option 2 — Mission‑Based Colony Builder (Sequential Missions Only)**

* **Gameplay depth:** Strong at scenario design (Apollo‑style landing missions, specific Artemis‑like sorties), lighter on long‑term planning.  
* **Educational value:** Very good for illustrating landing hazards, sun/Earth visibility, EVA planning, but may underplay long‑term programme trade‑offs.  
* **Scientific credibility:** High per‑mission; risk of implying that a handful of spectacular missions equals “sustained presence”.  
* **Technical complexity:** High for mission simulation, path‑planning, surface operations AI, etc.; lower for macro systems.  
* **Reusability of existing engine:** Excellent at the mission level; can fully exploit terrain, visibility timelines, site comparison.  
* **Suitability for teachers/public:** Good for short classroom sessions (“Here’s your landing site; plan a safe EVA”), but lacks the sense of a programme unfolding over years.

### **Option 3 — Hybrid Programme Manager \+ Mission Simulator**

* **Gameplay depth:** Highest; strategic layer (budgets, TRL, mission design, site selection, timing) plus tactical/operational “slices” of key missions.  
* **Educational value:** Strongest overall—can show how long‑term architectural decisions manifest in specific operational dilemmas (e.g., your choice of arrival date now forces a dusk landing with marginal power).  
* **Scientific credibility:** High, as long as the mission‑level is carefully scoped (e.g., simplified lander fuel margins, coarse EVA models) and clearly distinguished from actual certification‑grade simulation.  
* **Technical complexity:** Highest; requires both robust management layer and carefully designed mission vignettes, but those vignettes can be relatively lightweight and reused across campaigns.  
* **Reusability of existing engine:** Maximised; the same 3D/visibility engine supports both site‑selection planning tools and in‑mission visualisation.  
* **Suitability for teachers/public:** Strong; teachers can focus on strategy while dipping into missions as case studies; curious players get both big‑picture and hands‑on experiences.

**Recommendation:** Pursue **Option 3 — Hybrid** for Stargazer Mission Mode. It leverages the existing scientific engine most fully, aligns with the project’s emphasis on south‑pole lighting and communications geometry, and best communicates that sustainable presence is about **architecture under constraints** rather than isolated heroic landings.

---

**9Part 9 — Proposed First Campaign (MVP‑Scale)**

This campaign is deliberately compact: \~5–7 strategic turns (each representing several months) and 2–3 small operational mission segments.

### **Milestone 1 — Select a Candidate South‑Pole Region**

* **Player objective:** Choose a primary landing region for Phase I robotic operations.  
* **Required projects:**  
  * “Orbital Survey 1” (using pre‑existing LRO‑like data; abstracted for MVP).  
* **Resources consumed:** Small initial budget; 1 “survey” mission slot.  
* **Time required:** 1–2 in‑game turns (fictional but fixed assumption).  
* **Dependencies:** None (starting point).  
* **Setbacks:** If player chooses without sufficient surveying, hidden hazards increase future landing risk.  
* **Success conditions:** Select a region balancing:  
  * Minimum threshold of annual illumination on nearby ridges,  
  * Reasonable Earth‑visibility fraction,  
  * Proximity to PSRs (science interest).  
* **Unlocks:** Visibility timelines, horizon masks, and hazard overlays for that region in strategic UI.

### **Milestone 2 — Robotic Reconnaissance Lander**

* **Player objective:** Land a small robotic mission to refine terrain hazards and lighting at a specific site within the region.  
* **Required projects:**  
  * Small cargo lander family R at TRL sufficient for uncrewed use.  
  * Basic direct‑to‑Earth comms system.  
* **Resources:** Moderate budget; 1 rocket slot; use of launch window.  
* **Time:** 1 turn development, 1 turn for launch & operations (game assumption).  
* **Dependencies:** Completion of Milestone 1\.  
* **Potential setbacks:**  
  * Launch scrub (delay into next window → different arrival lighting, shown via Stargazer engine).  
  * Landing failure if site too risky or if lander TRL low.  
* **Success conditions:** Lander survives and transmits:  
  * Local slope/hazard data,  
  * Actual sun/Earth visibility timeline (refining models).  
* **Unlocks:** Reduced landing‑risk variance at that site; first modest increase in “Power knowledge” and “Comms knowledge”.

### **Milestone 3 — Lander Development & Test**

* **Player objective:** Develop a medium‑capacity cargo lander capable of delivering power/comm infrastructure.  
* **Required projects:**  
  * “Cargo Lander C” design and environmental test.  
* **Resources:** Significant budget; occupies 1–2 project slots for multiple turns.  
* **Time:** 2–3 turns for development and one uncrewed test flight.  
* **Dependencies:** Base level of launch infrastructure; at least one robotic landing experience (for realistic constraints).  
* **Setbacks:**  
  * Cost/schedule overrun (abstracted dice roll modifiable by prior investment).  
  * Test‑flight anomaly requiring redesign (adds extra turn).  
* **Success conditions:** A successful test landing within some distance of intended target.  
* **Unlocks:** Capability to land heavier infrastructure (power units, comm towers, small habitat modules).

### **Milestone 4 — Deliver Initial Power or Communications System**

Player chooses one of two branches for MVP (or does both with more difficulty):

#### 4A — Power‑First

* **Objective:** Deploy a solar power array on a well‑illuminated ridge.  
* **Required projects:**  
  * “South‑Pole Solar Array 1” (design).  
  * Optional “Mast/Tower 1” to increase illumination fraction.  
* **Dependencies:** Cargo Lander C; site knowledge from Milestone 2\.  
* **Setbacks:**  
  * If arrival date misaligned, initial operations hampered by shadowed conditions; arrays produce only partial power.  
* **Success conditions:** Achieve base‑power capacity threshold (e.g., can support one uncrewed station plus future small habitat).  
* **Unlocks:** Power budget in strategic layer, enabling permanent instruments or small habitat.

#### 4B — Comms‑First

* **Objective:** Deploy a surface comms tower or small relay orbiter serving the region.  
* **Required projects:**  
  * “Relay 1” (surface tower or single orbiter).  
* **Dependencies:** Lander/TRM; orbital‑mechanics model (simplified).  
* **Setbacks:**  
  * Coverage less than expected due to local terrain (revealed by Stargazer horizon).  
* **Success conditions:** Raise minimum comms uptime at intended base site to target threshold (e.g., 60%).  
* **Unlocks:** Safer later crew operations; higher allowable EVA durations.

### **Milestone 5 — Establish First Surface Outpost Node**

* **Player objective:** Emplace a small uncrewed outpost module at or near the eventual base site (e.g., logistics node or uncrewed habitat precursor).  
* **Required projects:**  
  * “Uncrewed Logistics Node” or “Habitat Demo 1” (short‑duration pressurised module with minimal ECLSS).  
* **Resources:** Large cargo‑lander mission.  
* **Dependencies:** Sufficient power at site (if uncrewed habitat), or minimum comms coverage (if remote operations).  
* **Setbacks:**  
  * Outpost life‑limit exceeded if power insufficent during long night (you lose some invested infrastructure).  
* **Success conditions:** Outpost survives one full synodic month of operation according to simplified power/thermal model (fed by real sun‑visibility curve but internalised with fictional assumptions).  
* **Unlocks:** Raises life‑support TRL; provides cargo‑staging point for future crewed mission.

### **Milestone 6 — Prepare for Initial Crewed or Extended Robotic Operation**

For MVP, you may end before actual crewed landing; the goal is to **be ready**.

* **Player objective:** Achieve readiness gate: “Capable of supporting a 14‑day crewed sortie” or “Capable of running a continuous robotic operation for 6 months”.  
* **Required projects:**  
  * For crewed: human‑rated lander, suit TRL, operations protocols, emergency shelter configuration.  
  * For extended robotic: robust comms, redundant power, at least one mobility system.  
* **Dependencies:** Earlier milestones; specific thresholds in Power, Comms, Habitats, Human Ops tech trees.  
* **Setbacks:** Time pressure from “political” objective (soft deadline); missing it reduces next‑campaign starting budget.  
* **Success conditions:** Pass an automated “readiness check” that ensures you have closed defined capability gaps.  
* **Unlocks:** End‑of‑campaign scoring; narrative hook for next campaign (“First Crew to Shackleton Rim”).

This campaign is just complex enough to exercise Stargazer’s unique engine and the architecture/trade‑off logic, but small enough for an MVP.

**10Part 10 — Technical Handover**

### **10.1 Existing Stargazer Capabilities**

* 3D lunar surface visualisation for the south pole.  
* Integration with LOLA‑derived DEMs.  
* Terrain horizon calculation from arbitrary surface locations.  
* Sun and Earth position calculation.  
* Visibility timelines over a synodic month (\~29.53 days).  
* Site comparison tools between locations.

### **10.2 Features That Can Be Reused**

* **Horizon and visibility engine:** Directly drive:  
  * Illumination fraction curves for chosen sites.  
  * Earth‑visibility curves for communications planning.  
* **3D viewport:** Used both in strategic site selection and in mission vignettes (e.g., lander approach visualisation, EVA planning).  
* **Comparison panel:** Repurposed as a “site trade‑study” tool comparing candidate base regions.

### **10.3 New Calculations Required (Engine‑Adjacent, Not Full Simulation)**

* **Derived power envelopes:** Given sun‑visibility vs time and a notional fixed solar array, approximate available electrical power vs time (using **explicitly fictional** assumptions: e.g., fixed peak kW, ideal cosine law, no dust/degradation).  
* **Comms coverage envelopes:** Given Earth‑visibility vs time and presence/absence of simple relay nodes, classify periods into “direct”, “relay”, or “blackout” for UI; no detailed link‑budget calculation initially.  
* **Risk scores:** For each site, combine slope statistics and roughness data (if available) into a qualitative landing‑hazard rating.

### **10.4 New Game Simulation Systems Required**

* **Strategic calendar and event system:** Months/years, annotated with launch windows (abstracted) and polar illumination for selected targets.  
* **Project management layer:** Project slots, durations, dependencies, cost abstraction, TRL progression.  
* **Mission resolution layer:** Simplified models for:  
  * Launch success/scrub (using weather \+ technical chance).  
  * Landing success based on hazard rating and lander reliability.  
  * Infrastructure performance over time using power/comms envelopes.  
* **Stateful infrastructure model:** Track assets at each lunar site (arrays, towers, outposts), their health, and cumulative “dust burden.”  
* **UI for tech trees and capability gates** reflecting Moon Base functions.

### **10.5 Features to Exclude From MVP**

* Detailed thermal modelling.  
* Particle‑level dust dynamics or CFD‑grade plume modelling.  
* Real radio‑frequency link budgets and modulation/coding schemes.  
* Full EVA kinematics or rover path‑planning.  
* Realistic budgeting with \$ accuracy; use abstracted “funds” and “launch capacity” instead.

These can be left for P1/P2 expansions without compromising educational value.

---

**11Part 11 — Prioritised Development Recommendations**

### **P0 — Essential for First Playable**

1. **Strategic Calendar & Site‑Selection Integration**  
   * *Rationale:* Core to the game’s identity; connects programme decisions to sun/Earth visibility.  
   * *Acceptance:* Player can select a south‑pole site; UI displays monthly illumination and Earth‑visibility curves derived from existing engine; arrival‑date slider shows changing conditions.  
2. **Basic Project/Tech System with Dependencies**  
   * *Rationale:* Needed to represent phased progression and TRL‑like gating.  
   * *Acceptance:* Player can start, track, and complete projects; projects require prerequisites; locked projects clearly show unmet dependencies.  
3. **Abstracted Mission Resolver Using Physics‑Informed Inputs**  
   * *Rationale:* To turn decisions into outcomes without full physics sim.  
   * *Acceptance:* Launches can succeed/fail or scrub; landings succeed probabilistically with modifiers from hazard rating and lander TRL; infrastructure operates with uptime driven by power/comms envelopes.  
4. **Infrastructure & Capability Tracking**  
   * *Rationale:* To measure progress toward readiness gate.  
   * *Acceptance:* Game tracks power capacity, comms uptime, habitat capability; readiness check for Milestone 6 responds to these metrics.  
5. **MVP UI/UX for Mission Mode**  
   * *Rationale:* Coherent experience separate from current analysis mode.  
   * *Acceptance:* Clear separation between planning layer and 3D inspection layer; tutorials explain difference between illumination vs power, Earth visibility vs comms.

### **P1 — Important Future Additions**

1. **Mission‑Level Vignettes**  
   * *Rationale:* To humanise outcomes and teach local terrain effects.  
   * *Acceptance:* At least two mission scenes (e.g., lander landing zone selection, short EVA planning) where the player interacts in the 3D scene and decisions feed back into strategic layer.  
2. **More Detailed Power & Dust Modelling**  
   * *Rationale:* To highlight degradation and maintenance decisions.  
   * *Acceptance:* Solar assets accrue dust; dust reduces effective power; dust‑mitigation tech reduces rate.  
3. **Expanded Tech Trees Reflecting Moon Base Functional Requirements**  
   * *Rationale:* To align more tightly with NASA categories.  
   * *Acceptance:* Power, habitat, mobility, ISRU trees explicitly tied to labelled functions (FN‑P‑101, FN‑H‑101, etc., as flavour text).  
4. **Multiple Regions and Comparative Architectures**  
   * *Rationale:* To teach that different south‑pole regions have different trade spaces.  
   * *Acceptance:* Player can run campaigns in at least two different regions with clearly different illumination/PSR/comms profiles.

### **P2 — Optional Expansions**

1. **Economic/Commercial Dimension**  
   * *Rationale:* To explore CLPS 2.0‑style commercial ecosystems.  
   * *Acceptance:* Optional scenario where private providers and lunar commerce change constraints.  
2. **ISRU‑Centric Campaigns**  
   * *Rationale:* To deep‑dive into resource‑driven architectures.  
   * *Acceptance:* Campaign built around demonstrating water/oxygen ISRU and propellant depots, with more detailed ISRU tech model.  
3. **Multi‑Agency/International Coordination**  
   * *Rationale:* To reflect international partnerships (e.g., JAXA rover, ESA relays).  
   * *Acceptance:* Systems to negotiate shared infrastructure and different political objectives.

---

**12Part 12 — Presentation Summary**

**Short game pitch:**  
*Stargazer: Moonbase Architect* is a single‑player strategy game where you direct a realistic lunar exploration programme at the Moon’s south pole. Using real NASA terrain data and orbital geometry, you must plan missions, build infrastructure, and manage risk on a path from first robotic lander to a viable outpost.

**Main player objective:**  
Achieve readiness for sustained south‑pole operations by closing key capability gaps—power, communications, habitats, and environmental knowledge—while working within constrained budgets, launch windows, and technology risks.

**Central gameplay conflict:**  
Do you push aggressively for early, headline‑grabbing capabilities (like a large habitat or ambitious ISRU plant) at higher risk of failures and overruns, or build more cautiously through many robotic precursors and incremental tech maturation, potentially missing political or funding windows?

**Strongest three educational lessons:**

1. **Environment as first‑order driver:** Illumination, Earth visibility, and terrain at the south pole directly shape where and how a base can exist; they are not cosmetic details but architectural constraints.  
2. **Capability‑driven phasing:** Sustainable presence arises from a sequence of capabilities (mapping → landers → power/comms → habitats → ISRU), each dependent on prior technology readiness and infrastructure.  
3. **Programme‑level risk management:** Delays, budget overruns, and technology uncertainty are intrinsic; good architectures hedge, use pathfinders, and avoid single points of failure.

**How Stargazer’s existing scientific engine makes the game distinctive:**

* Real LOLA‑derived topography and horizon calculations drive illumination and Earth‑visibility timelines, so every site‑selection or launch‑timing decision is grounded in real celestial geometry.  
* The same 3D visualisation used for educational analysis becomes an in‑game planning and mission‑ops tool, allowing players to see exactly **why** a chosen ridge gets more sunlight or a crater blocks Earth.  
* This tight coupling between authentic environmental modelling and strategic decisions creates a management game where the “board” is the actual Moon, and where players genuinely learn how real agencies think about building a lunar foothold.
